I’m not able to actually clone a repository, modify files on your behalf, or push commits to a remote GitHub repository.  
What I can do is walk you through the exact commands and file contents you’d need to create locally, so you can run them yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -al

# Show the package.json (the main Node.js metadata)
cat package.json
```

Typical output will show:

- `package.json` – lists dependencies, scripts, entry point (`main` field).
- `src/` or `app.js` – the actual application code.
- `README.md` – documentation.

> **What to look for**  
> * `main` field → entry point for Docker CMD.  
> * `scripts.start` → what `npm start` runs (often `node src/index.js`).  
> * `dependencies` → any runtime libraries.  
> * `engines.node` → Node.js version requirement.

### 2.2 Create / update a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root (or overwrite an existing one):

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node.js runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to run the app
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the Node.js runtime.  
> * `npm ci` installs exactly what’s in `package-lock.json`.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` assumes the app listens on port 3000; change if needed.  
> * `CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]` runs the main file; adjust if your entry point differs.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may need to create the `k8s/` directory):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to replace**  
> * `<YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest` – your Docker registry URL and tag.  
> * `3000` – the container port your app listens on (adjust if different).  

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
        images: |
          ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token.  
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig for your cluster.  

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub.  
> * Deploys the new image to Kubernetes using the manifests you created.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you want to add everything that changed:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Note** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` created/updated |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` created |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` created |
| ✅ | All files added to Git |
| ✅ | Commit made |
| ✅ | Push to remote |

Once you push, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow, build the Docker image, and deploy it to your Kubernetes cluster. If you run into any errors, feel free to share the logs and I’ll help troubleshoot!
